reason: The chambers need muscle to squeeze blood, as the goal describes.
expectation: The heart muscle will surround the chambers so they can squeeze.

effect: The chambers can squeeze, but fluid currently moves toward both openings, so they need a way to direct the flow.
reaction: The two-way arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The valve picture shows them closing against reverse flow, which should help drive blood forward.
expectation: The valves will direct blood forward when the chambers squeeze.

effect: The valves direct flow during squeezing and allow the chambers to refill. The pump still needs repeated squeezes.
reaction: The squeeze and refill panels clarify how the valves work.
reason: The pacemaker cells produce a spreading electrical wave, suggesting they can coordinate repeated heart squeezes.
expectation: The pacemaker cells will help the heart squeeze repeatedly.

effect: The pacemaker cells produced a beating heart, completing the goal of repeated forward squeezes. The remaining goal needs blood and a returning vessel route.
reaction: The distinction between the heart starting its own beat and nerves adjusting it is interesting.
reason: The red-cell envelopes have room for hemoglobin, whose binding sites can carry oxygen.
expectation: Hemoglobin will fill the envelopes to make oxygen-carrying red blood cells.

effect: The red blood cells contain hemoglobin and make ATP from sugar without mitochondria. They can now be added to plasma to make blood.
reaction: The cells making ATP without mitochondria is an interesting contrast with the muscle cells.
reason: Plasma is the fluid part of blood, so combining it with red blood cells should provide blood for the returning route.
expectation: The red blood cells will be suspended in plasma to make blood.

effect: The red blood cells and plasma form oxygen-carrying blood, ready to be fitted into a circulation route.
reaction: The inset clarifies that other blood components are included too.
reason: Capillary networks can connect arteries and veins into a route that returns blood to the heart.
expectation: The capillaries will join the arteries and veins into a continuous vessel network.

effect: The capillaries connected the arteries and veins into a circuit with slots for a pump and transport medium.
reaction: The marked slots make the remaining assembly clear.
reason: The beating heart supplies the pump needed for the vessel circuit.
expectation: The heart will fit into the circuit's pump slot.

effect: The beating heart is installed in the vessel circuit; the transport medium slot still needs blood.
reaction: The heart's connections make the returning route clear.
reason: Oxygen-carrying blood is the transport medium for the circuit.
expectation: The blood will fill the circuit's transport medium slot.

effect: Adding the blood completed the circuit and showed how it can deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissues while carrying carbon dioxide back.
reaction: The closed-loop picture connects the pump and vessels in a satisfying way.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding the valves was most worthwhile: the squeeze and refill panels explain how their opening and closing directs flow.

leastWorthwhile.text: Fitting the heart and then the blood was clear but predictable once the circuit showed its two named slots.

surprise.text: The red blood cells make ATP from sugar despite having no mitochondria, an interesting contrast with the earlier muscle cells.

arbitrary.text: No action felt particularly arbitrary; the pictures and goals gave each combination a clear purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the chapter connected familiar heart parts to their functions and introduced an interesting difference between red blood cells and muscle cells.
